sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: All right. Good morning again. Today is March 26, 2010, as we just said, and this is the beginning of a veteran's history interview with Mr. Dale Huss. Mr. Huss served as a pilot in World War II. I'm Katherine Gillen, the library director at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona. Mr. Huss and I are in the Luke Air Force Base Library. Mr. Huss, I understand you're from California.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yes, ma'am, Los Angeles, California.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's right. And you were born in 1925.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yes, on the twenty-six of....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So happy birthday, doubly involved here, yes! When you were in California, you had an early interest in aviation and airplanes. Can you talk about that a little bit?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, yes, we lived just a little bit south of the Glendale Airport, which in those days was LAX. LAX-Mines [phonetic] Field, didn't come about until during the war, really, and became LAX after the war, and they moved out of Glendale down there, because Glendale wasn't big enough to support the airline industry that Los Angeles was building. But when Glendale was LAX, it wasn't called LAX, it was just Los Angeles Airport in Glendale, California. When I was in high school, I worked there for the Tim Aircraft Company, which was a manufacturer. I worked as their line boy on the flight line. And we had such famous people from the movie industry that parked their airplanes there: Wallace Barry, for example, was one of our favorites, because when he came back from someplace, I was the one that always had to wipe his airplane down. So I became acquainted with people like Wallace Barry and Errol Flynn and those guys that flew their own airplanes, which in those days was, "Wow!"

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Uh-huh, very much so. So tell me about the first time you got to go in an airplane.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: I was about eight or nine years old. We were out at the airport on a Sunday afternoon, and there was a Ford Tri-motor there, that was selling rides. They were having difficulty selling the last seat, and the pilot wouldn't take off without the airplane being full. So my father approached the ticket seller and said, "Take all three of my kids for five dollars and you can fill that seat." And my little sister was smaller than me, and my brother was a little bit bigger than me, was two years older. But the guy looked at us and said, "Okay, it's a deal." So we went for a ride around Los Angeles and Glendale in a Ford Tri-motor, for five dollars, in the jump seat.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: All three of you?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: All three of us.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And your little sister was how old?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, let's see, she's six years [younger] than I am, so she was about three or four.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh my goodness! Of course your mother.... You said your mother was fine with that?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yes. My mother, when she graduated from Ann Arbor, University of Michigan, as an R.N., wanted to be a stewardess and fly for the airlines. She managed to get pregnant, and they didn't hire pregnant ladies in those days. But they hired only nurses in those days, so she had a lead in. But then nature happened, and it was gone. So she encouraged my flying ambitions.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: It was in the genes there!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, she wanted to fly. And it was my pleasure to take her flying after the war.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh! That must have been a great pleasure for her. We'll probably talk about that in a minute, or a little later. So what was your next opportunity for flying? It was kind of a big change when you were like fourteen?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. I was in high school and I was taking a public speaking course from a private school, lady instructor. And she had scheduled a recital. And my younger sister was taking lessons, and she was scheduled to perform. And I was taking public speaking, and I was scheduled to perform. And I had to write my own speech as part of the assignment. And I wrote a speech about the history of aviation. After the recital, (with emotion) a gentleman came up to me and wanted to know if I was interested in aviation. And I told him, "Yes, sir." And he said he was Joe Plauser [phonetic]. Well, I knew who Joe Plauser was, because he ran a flying school at Glendale Airport. And he said, "You know where my operation is?" And I said, "Yes." He said, "Well, come out there in the next couple of days and we'll go flying." So I did, the next day! We got in one of his instruction planes, it was a Piper, and we went flying. And I got to (with emotion) fly the airplane, to handle the controls, help on the landing, things like that. And I was impressed (with emotion) that it was definitely something I wanted to do.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: You were hooked!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Lassoed and grounded, you know!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That was a special moment there. Was that the last time you got to fly before the war then?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, I had another experience in a Ford Tri-motor when I went to San Francisco with my father on a business trip. We flew in a Ford to go to San Francisco. I enjoyed that. A Ford Tri-motor is a fantastic airplane. I've flown in the EAA's Ford a couple of times; and a couple of times in the right-hand co-pilot seat of the airplane. I didn't get to fly the airplane, but it was close enough to the action that I definitely knew what he was doing and why he was doing it, and how those old three reciprocals worked, because it was an old airplane. And so it was a pleasure to do that. I also got to fly the B-17 that belongs to the EAA, because I was an EAA volunteer at convention for about fourteen, fifteen years. Since I ran the trams from the flight line, volunteers from the campground to the flight line and back, when they were through with their tour, I was quite well known at EAA.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: But you were still in high school when Pearl Harbor hit?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: When the war started, I was in high school, and I think I was either a junior or a senior, I'm not really sure. But I was not very far away from graduation. Now oddly enough, I never did graduate from high school, because the Air Force wanted us to come and fly, and so I was signed up to do that. Well, I was just finishing my senior year, and L.A. City gave several of us our diplomas in advance, because we were going into the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh! So there was some special program that you could sign up in advance?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yes, the Navy had a program where they wanted pilot material, and they had solicited the schools to provide names of young men that could qualify to their requirements, which were quite stringent. You had to be like an "A" student, and had to have taken certain courses like physics and those type of things that are required for flying. And it was right after they discontinued the two-year college requirement, and you could volunteer, without going for two years, and they requested seniors in high school that could qualify. I went through their selection program, took three days, and I was there on the third day I was one of the three that was but they only took one of us, and I wasn't the one. So I went over to the Air Corps recruiting office, Sixth and Main in Los Angeles, and suggested I volunteer to them. And they asked if I was one of the 500, and I said, "Yes sir." "Were you there after the first day?" "Yes." "Were you there after the second day? Were you there after the third day?" "Yes, but I didn't get selected." And he handed me a piece of paper and said, "Sign there," and I was in the Air Corps! Those were the days. The war was the big thing in those days. Everybody wanted to be a soldier, everybody wanted to do their thing, and I had had the opportunity to do it, so I did.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So when did you first start your training? Where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: April of 19....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: April of 1943.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah, you would have been eighteen. Yeah. Just eighteen.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. We had to be eighteen years old, that was part of the deal.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah, you were just eighteen.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Let's see, my birthday was in March, and on the fourteenth of April, I received my orders and got on a choo-choo train up to Kerns, Utah, which was the basic entry base where you marched and learned how to be a soldier, got your shots, all that preliminary stuff. And from there, we were sent to Spearfish, South Dakota, to the Black Hills Teachers College, for college indoctrination, to try to pick up some of the stuff that maybe some of the boys didn't have. So we did chemistry, we did physics, and we did calculus, and we did English, because an Air Force pilot's supposed to be able to write, got to write reports, and things of that nature. We were there about three months, and they shortened that program and sent us to Santa Ana for classification. At classification you took a battery of tests all the way from physical exams that most of the guys had had to take before they got selected; but because the Navy had done all those things with me, I didn't have to do any of those things. At the end of the test period, the classification as they called it, we were given the opportunity to select the task that we wanted to pursue. If you were what they wanted as a pilot, you could sign up to be a pilot. If what they wanted was a navigator, you signed up to be a navigator. If they wanted you for a bombardier, you signed up to be a bombardier. Well, I was qualified for all three, so naturally I signed to be a pilot. Later I got into navigation and bombardiering, but that is another story, because that was after I was commissioned. So I selected pilot, and I got pilot. I was qualified to be all three, but I selected pilot and got pilot. And so after we finished pre-flight at Santa Ana, which was part of the cadet program prior to that time we'd been aviation students, now we are aviation cadets. Oh, and I should say that during college detachment training, we flew ten hours in Piper Cubs as an indoctrination to the flight program. And we had to write a report about each one of our flights, and it was a fun experience because up in South Dakota it's a beautiful place to fly especially low and slow, (chuckles) Anyway, after pre-flight, which was a full two-month part of the pilot program, I was sent to Dos Pelos, California, in pilots, where we flew Ryan PT-22s for two months. Then from there to Chico, and we flew two months there in BT-13s. And then to Luke Field for advanced, where we flew AT-6s, and graduated, and were assigned to a permanent duty slot. I was assigned as a contract flying school supervisor to Ryan School of Aeronautics in Hemet, California.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Let's back up a little bit, since we're here at Luke, tell me some of your impressions. What was it like here? You said you came here for advanced training.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So let's talk about that a little bit. What was that like, and what was Luke like?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, Luke was a great place, because it was the finish of what we were all trying to do become pilots. We did it here. We graduated here, and Luke had T-6s that we were flying, and the T-6 is a beautiful airplane. And of course Phoenix is right over there, and Phoenix, even then, was a great town. It wasn't a very big town, but it was a great town, and it was a good weekend leave type town. We'd go to town and stay at the Hotel Adams, which got torn down a few years ago. Adams Hotel was on Adams Boulevard, right across the street from the newspaper office. It was not an old hotel, but it was not a new hotel either. They had a good restaurant, and the town had excellent restaurants, so we could do things to enjoy ourselves on weekends, and go back on Sunday nights for Monday morning flight line. And we flew every day during the week, and the weekend go back to Phoenix for recreation. So it was a wonderful assignment.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: How many hours a day were you flying?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Golly, it depended on where we were in our program. Before you soloed, you flew once a day with your instructor, and you flew about an hour. As you got into the program, you started shooting landings. And then we had instrument training. And we transferred to another squadron for instrument flying. We did cross-country work. Arizona's a beautiful area to go cross-country. It is just real pretty.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Beautiful state.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: We'd fly out to Globe, and then down to.... Oh, that town down there there used to be a primary school.... Douglas! And then over to Casa Grande, and back to Luke and land cross-country. And that usually took a couple three hours to do. As we got further into the program and were soloing a lot, we flew about a hundred hours at Luke, for a total of—you had to have at least 200, which in those days was the license requirement for commercial license. I had 210 when I finished my training and graduated, and I ended up with a commercial license. I still carry it. I don't use it, but I still carry it. And Luke was a great experience: nice people, everybody was friendly, everybody wanted to do something for you, including the instructors.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah. But it was fairly intense training, though, I would think. Was it a fairly intense type of training?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yes. You flew every day, just about. If you're going to grab 100 hours in two months, you've got to fly. And so we did: we flew, we flew, we flew.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: You kind of mentioned all the places you had more basic training before the final flight training. Was there an accident or something along those lines when you were in your second phase of flight training?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: At basic training I had a mid-air collision.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: You want to tell us about that a little bit?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: (chuckles) Yeah, I suppose, if you want to hear it.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh, I definitely want to hear it.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: It was during night flight, and in basic training you fly in a zone. You take off and you're assigned a zone and quadrant: Like in Zone 3, which was the third guy up; and the second quadrant was in the second quadrant, third guy up. So you you're assigned a place, and you take off and fly to that place. And they call an airplane in to come in and make a landing, night landing, take off, go back to your zone. Well, I was called to come in from my zone to make a landing. So I went for the pattern, came around, and was on final approach, with everything in sight, and made a final approach, when I got the impression to look to my left. And I looked left, and there was a wing coming at me! (laughs) It was another airplane that was turning final approach and he hadn't been called, incidentally but he was turning final approach. And his wingtip came down on my canopy, took my windshield off, took the prop off, and we both crash landed at the field. Now I didn't have any power left, and so I was short of the field, and it was muddy, so I left my landing gear out on the muddy field, and bounded up onto the runway and skidded down the runway, which closed the field for the night. But anyway, they determined that I was not hurt, and so they bused me back to the base, because this is being done at an auxiliary field. And the next day, they gave assignments to fly, and I didn't get one. I was accustomed at this time to being assigned to fly something, because we'd fly during the day, and then fly at night. So I didn't get an assignment. So I'm sitting in the ready room all by myself, because everybody else is flying, and a colonel came into the room and said, "Anybody here want to go for a ride?" And I said, "I do!" Raised my hand. We went for a fly, and he got in the back seat and told me what to do, and he wanted me to fly him an instrument pattern, and this would give him an instrument flight. So we went up and did the AV pattern series, and then he said, "Okay, go back to the field." So I went back and landed, and he thanked me and went away. A little bit after that, my squadron commander came in, and he asked me if I volunteered to go flying. I said, "Yes sir." He said, "Do you know who you were flying with?" I said, "No sir. He's a colonel." And he said, "Well, he's the head of the instrument school at Santa Ana, and he tells us what to do when we're training for instruments." And I said, "Oh. Okay." I'm in trouble! My squadron commander said, "You gave him such a good flight that I can't eliminate you and you were eliminated." But I was retained and got a real high rating on my instrument training. Instrument flying for me was easy. You just believed what the panel told you. That's all you had to do, was just believe what it tells you. Don't decide it doesn't know what it's telling you. And so I got out of Chico with a good score in instruments, and a good score in flying, and went to Luke Field for advanced.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That was amazing. I was hearing that story, though, you said that the wing knocked your canopy off. You almost got decapitated!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, I ducked. When I saw it coming, I ducked! I just whipped down in the cockpit, and it went "crash!" right over my head, and (thpptt!) off goes the top of the windshield.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh my gosh!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. His engine went through my wingtip and took about three feet off of it.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And this was a T-6 as well?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: No, no, this was a BT-13.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: BT-13, okay. And what base was this at?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Chico, northern San Joaquin Valley. It's a junior college nowadays.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah, I've heard of that. Oh my goodness. You had an awesome time here, though, at Luke with the training.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Where did [you] go from there?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: My assignment from Luke was to go to Ryan Hemet, California as a contract flying school supervisor. And our job there.... Contract flying schools were civilian schools. Ryan Aeronautics of San Diego, which started in San Diego before the war, built the field up at Hemet because they had to get out of San Diego because there were too many B-24s being built there, and the sky was crowded. So they built Hemet. It was a civilian school, all the instructors were civilian, the management of the school was civilian. It was a contractor. And the Air Force put well, there were fourteen of us there as supervisors, and I was one of the flying supervisors. So we had ground instructors as supervisors, supervising the civilian ground instructors. I was required to do some of that too, but basically we were there to make sure that the contractor provided the level of instruction that the Air Force was paying for. We had to supervise the flight criteria. We had to carry five students ourselves, just because we were there and didn't have a full schedule, you might say. Okay, you fly with five students. So I learned an awful lot doing that, because if you can teach flying, you can fly; and if you can fly, you can teach it if you know what you're flying. And it is a very learning experience, to teach someone else how to fly. So I learned a lot. I was doing it, but you don't really think about what you're doing, until you try to teach somebody else how to do it.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's very true.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Then you really learn it. And I enjoyed Hemet. It was a wonderful job. (with emotion) It's probably the best job I ever had, anyplace, and I've had some good jobs!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Could you pretty well tell when you had a good student?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yes! Yes. I had a student that did not require any instructions. He had never been in an airplane before, but he was what we call a natural pilot. You showed him something once, he did it. You didn't have to show him anything twice. So you could show him everything, and he could do everything that you had shown him. We weren't allowed to fly any acrobatics with them, but a snap roll here and there helps a lot, and he could do snap rolls! When he went to basic, he was a pilot already. His name was Richard Hayes.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Did you ever follow up on him, find out....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: We wrote for probably about six months while he was going through the rest of his cadets. He came here to Luke. Because I had advised him that being a fighter pilot was what he needed to do, because he was such a natural flyer, "Be a fighter pilot. The airplane will live with you, and you will own it."

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: True. Did you ever have to flunk anybody, tell them, "Hey, you're not meant to fly"?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, I had a couple of students that I had to serve elimination on, yes. If the school decided somebody needed to be eliminated, we had to check them to see whether they were supposed to be eliminated or not. (aside about allergies) So anyway, yes, the school would then send well, the first place the instructor would send the student would be to the squadron commander, who was a civilian in charge of the squadron. And if the squadron commander agreed with the instructor, he would send that student to what we called "the Army." And that was us. We were the Army check pilots. And we would ride with that student and decide to accept the elimination and eliminate him the decision was ours or to retain that student. We could retain him ourselves, but we were only allowed to carry five students, so we always had to pass on some student to another instructor so that we could provide a vacancy for that student that we wanted to work with. So in my several months there, I had about three or four previously assigned elimination students that I was working with. The ones that we agreed that we could then pass on, if we got them far enough along that we thought that they could pass the examination, we would pass them to another squadron, and the Army guy over there would fly them, and decide to agree with us, or not agree with us. If he agreed with us that the student should be retained, he was assigned to a different squadron than what he had been in, so that his ex-instructor couldn't influence his new instructor. He was separated from where he first got eliminated. So it was a tough decision that had to be made, but yes, we did salvage several students at the school, because the school got I know I shouldn't say this the school got paid for the number of students that they successfully got through, and the instructor got paid for how many hours he flew. If he was tired of flying and we had some of those and wanted to cut his work load, he'd eliminate one of his students, just put him up for elimination. That's what we had to watch for, was this one of those that's coming in here because the instructor is tired? Because, you know, the instructors were awful busy. They were very, very busy. And teaching flying is not an easy job. It's work, it takes a lot of concentration, and it's physical. Of course you never know when a student's going to make a wrong move. You're always there. If you're flying with a student, you're always right on the control column. You've got your fingers around it, you just aren't touching it the column. You can grab it quickly, take over, save the day, whatever is necessary. It's a pressure job that you're involved every time you're in the airplane. And of course then we also had to do ground school inspection. We'd have to go to ground school and make sure the instructor was teaching the course right, things like that. It was things that we had learned when we were in the primary school series ourselves. So we knew what we were hearing, and we just had to make sure we were hearing the right thing. And sometimes our ground school instructors weren't the best. It was ... a bit rough.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: How long were you there, doing that job?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, golly, I left there in November. I went there in July and I left in November, about six months. We got selected by our commanding officer, who was a major. I got selected for a training program for the P-59, which was the first jet airplane built by Bell. We were to go to Fresno and Hammer [phonetic] Field, and fly the airplane, and write the training syllabus for the students that would be coming to learn how to fly that airplane. The airplane was brand new, unheard of. It wasn't even publicly acknowledged that there was such a thing as a jet, and so nobody knew anything. We ranked from major we had two majors and several first lieutenants, and a whole bunch of second lieutenants that were in this thirty-person cadre to do this assignment. Okay, we were briefed as to what the assignment was, we were sent to Luke Field to re-shoot our gunnery, because they wanted gunnery up to date, (pause) Can I use the fellow's name?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Okay, (pause) Huh, I can't remember the colonel's name who was director of training!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: It'll pop into your head in a second.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, it'll come to me. But anyway.... Colonel Cox!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: There you go!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Colonel Cox gathered us in the ready room. He had read what we were doing and what we were being assigned to. He said, "You people are not going to get that assignment. As long as none of my instructors were selected, you don't get to go." So he flew his P-51 down to Santa Ana, got with some important people down there, came back, and had in his hand our orders, changed. We were reassigned. Well, our two majors got a T-6 and flew down to Santa Ana and got our orders reinstated. And then Colonel Cox flew to Santa Ana and got them cancelled again. And he came back and he grounded all of us and restricted us to base, so the two majors couldn't get an airplane to go to Santa Ana again.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Why was [Lt. Col. Cox] doing this kept canceling it?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Because none of his instructors had been selected for the program, and he felt they would be better for him.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And he thought you guys were young whippersnappers?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. Well, you know, he's looking at some second lieutenants and some first lieutenants and a couple of majors, and that's a pretty high-peak job. But in our book, Santa Ana, head of the training command, is supposed to know what they're doing. And they obviously had a plan, but they were being usurped by somebody over above them. When Cox would get down there, he had "buddies," you might say, and he'd get the orders direct to change, then come back with changed orders. Well, our majors went back to the people that had originally made the assignment, to select out the people that were going. I was selected by my major, my commanding officer. And he said.... Back when I was a student in primary myself, my instructor and this is my final 66-2 (with emotion) wrote "excellent instructor material" on my 66-2. That's why I didn't get to go to P-39s, and was assigned to a contract flying school, because that's where instruction starts. So anyway, he selected me out of all the militaries that we had on the base that would have been equally qualified, to do this job, because of what was in my 66-2. So anyway, Cox went back, got the orders changed, grounded us so we couldn't do anything about it, and we were assigned to Victorville Air Force Base to become radar navigator bombardiers. Victorville at that time was the mickey school. "Mickey" is what you call a radar operator. The machine was a "mickey." We were to become mickey operators. Well, you know, what the heck, that's not flying an airplane! So every one of us that was in that school that had come from that origin where they were really pilots and were being trained in this other duty, we all wrote our congressmen. Orders came to "Reassign those people. We paid to train them as pilots."

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: So we were assigned to B-24s, Albuquerque, New Mexico. We piloted B-24s, we passed our requirements to be a pilot in the B-24s. We were assigned as first pilot B-24s, and sent back to Victorville, because we knew radar and bombing, navigation. We were almost finished with all three of those schools when we got reassigned. But anyway, we knew what those techniques were. So we were flying B-24s at Victorville that were being used as mickey airplanes, with mickey students, to train those students how to fly a mickey mission and drop bombs. So we flew to places like Boulder Dam, at night, back and forth for nine hours back and forth, back and forth. Nine hours is a nine-hour mission over in Europe. So we were simulating a European mission in a B-24 squadron, as the lead airplane, with the mickey system installed in it. We also had B-l 7s with the mickey operation. Now, I wasn't flying B-l7s at that time that came later. Anyway, we were flying these B-24s and we'd fly out over the Channel Islands, and then up the Channel Island series to Falcon Island up there, and then come back in and "bomb" the Golden Gate Bridge, and fly down California. And we were "bombing" Hammer Field, incidentally. And then back to Victorville and land, completes the mission. We were flying daytime missions and nighttime missions, and we sometimes flew two missions a day: that's nine hours, twice a day. We logged a lot of time.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: A lot of time.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: But it wasn't the kind of time that any of us wanted, because almost every one of us was a trained fighter pilot at Luke Field or someplace in Texas that was training fighter pilots, or something like that, and had been reassigned to this, and got bounced and got stuck into this other task.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Do you think at the time it was just because somebody back in Washington decided, "Hey, right now, at this point in the war, we need more bomber pilots than we need fighter pilots"? Do you know if that was the thinking?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, I think that was part of it, that they agreed that we needed bomber pilots. We certainly needed mickey operators, and they needed an airplane to train them in, and somebody had to fly them, so we were flying them.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: What was it like to get into a B-24 after flying T-6s?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh! a B-24 is a truck! It is heavy on the controls, particularly in the aileron. It's cold and damp because you're flying at very high altitude. We were flying at 30,000 feet of altitude, and that's where the airlines fly nowadays.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: But without pressurization.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: No pressurization, and no decent heat, and the heated flight suits that didn't work. It was cold up there! (laughs)

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Those real heavy ones that you see?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, those fleece-lined leather jobs, with a piece of underwear underneath it that was wired like a blanket or sleeping bag, you know. It plugged into the thing on the side of the cockpit, and they didn't work worth a darn. Didn't care what the Air Force did, the pilots were cold. Everybody on the airplane was cold. Then one day I was assigned an airplane number, and we went and found the airplane. It was a B-17. Well, I wasn't checked out on B-17s, so I called Johnny Pollock [phonetic], my squadron commander.... And I saw Johnny Pollock again when one of our Air Force pilots put one of our F-89s into the mud flats up at Hamilton Field, and Northrop, when I was working for Northrop, and they sent me up there with a load of drawings, because Pollock's organization had decided the airplane was to be repaired. And so I took a load of drawings up there so that they could figure out what they needed to order, because the fuselage was virtually destroyed, because when it went into the mud, both engines went through the nacelle and out the tail end, from the mud pressure. And they were going to have to rebuild the fuselage, so they needed parts from Northrop, and I was assigned to identify the parts for them. In those days I was in spare parts administration.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's a little ahead, in the fifties?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. But anyway, it came in handy. Gillen : The same gentleman, Pollock.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Right, Johnny "Hot" Pollock on the radio. I called him up and said, "There's a problem." He said, "What's the problem?" I said, "This airplane you gave me is a B-17, and I'm not checked in B-17s. I'm not authorized [unclear]." So anyway he said, "What's the matter, Dale, you afraid to fly that airplane?" I called him a name. I said, "You know I'm not afraid to fly anything!" He said, "Then fly it!" So we did. We got the engineer to give me the pilot's manual, and we checked all the settings that we were going to need, and I told him he could stay back if he wanted to. He said, "This is my airplane, and where it goes, I go!" You know, flight engineers are very authoritative, they own that airplane, and you aren't going to do anything to it that they don't approve! So anyway, I told him, "Okay, you can stay on board. Just remember, we've never flown a B-17 before."

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Now, this is the same day, after you've just reviewed the pilot's manual, the flight manual, for a few hours or so?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah, we were on the airplane, reading the pilot's manual, checking the instruments. "We use this one, this one, and this one." Okay, so we fired the airplane up, taxied out. Oh, I left all of the students back there. I sent them back to the ready room, because I wasn't going to fly students on an airplane I hadn't flown. So anyway, we sent them back to operations which Johnny approved, incidentally. And we fired up, flew the airplane, flew the mission, which was an eight-hour mission. We flew the complete mission without the trainees, came back, landed, parked it, went in, and threw my parachute up on the counter and I said, "There! I flew your damned airplane!" He said, "Fine, now you're a B-17 pilot." (laughter)

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Which is probably what he wanted all along, right?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah, he wanted me to fly it. So I never flew another B-24, but I had several hundred hours in the B-24s at that time. I was an experienced B-24 pilot. So now I had to become an experienced B-17 pilot, because I had to fly students. Gillen : And how did it impress you when you first got into that plane?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: The 17? Well, the 17 was an easier airplane to fly. It was more stable, and it would behave itself, really. B-24 wouldn't behave itself: you had to stay with it and stay on it. But the 17 was a very calm airplane in the air. It didn't carry as many bombs as a B-24, so it wasn't as efficient a bomber as the B-24. We could get it to the same bombing altitude that they'd get the B-17s to, so it was just as efficient that way. It was faster than the B-17s, so over in Europe, the B-24s did not fly with the B-17s. They either were assigned to fly ahead or behind, because they were faster. And so the 17s, a lot of times, were leading missions in multiple airplanes hundreds of airplanes in one mission. And the B-24s were trailing. So by the time the B-17s got through with bomb dropping on Germany, here come the B-24s, and the Germans are all loaded to shoot them down. So the 24 was really a dangerous airplane in combat, because it was a burning airplane. If they'd get a shell into the fuselage, the thing would blow up because the gas always leaked. Convair had built a transfer system they called the U-tube. It was a rubber tube that you plugged into the transfer lines when you wanted to move fuel from the right wing to the left wing, for example. You plugged in the U-tube, and then you turned on the valves that moved the flow, and it went down through the U-tube and back up and over to the other wing. They leaked. They did not hold the fuel that was being transferred. It leaked. So Convair built a little catch pan underneath the bottom. Well, it would run down the U-tube and drop off into the bomb bay door. So the bomb bay was always full of fumes. You could smell it when you walked through, even at altitude. So they built a little pan with a line that went outside and vented overboard alongside of the airplane. So the fuel would drop into this pan and then run down this metal tube and out overboard. But in the meantime, it's collecting in this pan and it would evaporate, make fumes in the bomb bay. So if the Germans were able to get a shell into the bomb bay and they knew it the damned airplane would explode, because it's full of gasoline, the bomb bay is full of gasoline fumes.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: I didn't know that.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. So we called them "burners." We didn't like to transfer fuel. Of course we weren't being shot at in Victorville, but we didn't like having that fuel smell in the bomb bay. We had one airplane this is a diversion we had one airplane that had a fire on Engine No. 3. And they were coming back to Victorville and the pilot elected to send the copilot down to open the bomb bay so the crew could bail out over the base, because he was afraid the airplane wasn't going to be landable, really. Well, the copilot and the flight engineer went down and reached back in for the handle that opens the bomb bays, and opened the bomb bay and the airplane went "boom" right over the field. We're all out there watching, it's at nighttime. "Oh spectacular, we're going to see some fun!" And the thing went "boom" right up there, and all the pieces started coming down, and an engine landed right amidships of one of the B-24s parked on the line.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh my gosh!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: The only people that survived was the copilot and the flight engineer, because the explosion blew both of them out of the airplane. Everybody else died.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Did they have parachutes?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: They were getting ready to bail out. But the airplane blew, there was no way to get out, it's too late. They should not have opened the bomb bay.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh gosh.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Now this was an ex-combat pilot from Europe that was flying the airplane that night. He should have known better. But anyway....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's horrible.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: He should have never opened that bomb bay. But it was a very physical example of what you know. You know not to open the bomb bay, and that's why. And we were all out there. That's why. Spectacular. But anyway, the B-17, like I was saying, is an easy airplane to fly. I flew one about four years ago. Easy airplane to fly. In fact, on that flight four years ago.... Can I divert a little bit?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Sure! Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: On that flight four years ago in EAA, I flew the Aluminum Overcast on just a fun trip.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That was the name of the plane?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, the Aluminum Overcast. That's EAA's airplane. So being a volunteer at EAA and being well experienced at EAA, and associated with the flight department at EAA, what have you, I was volunteered to go flying with them. And I didn't have to pay for it, they charged for it, I didn't have to pay for it.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's awesome! Cost me like 400 bucks!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Five hundred! That's what we were charging in those days. But anyway, I told the guy that's responsible for the airplane, sitting in the co-pilot's seat, that I was going to make a steep turn to the left, do a 360, and level out. He said, "Okay. Go." So I cleared, started the turn, took it all the way around on a steep turn, didn't lose any altitude and that's important and when I came all the way out and started leveling out, I got that "boom! boom!" I had hit my prop wash, perfect turn.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: This is only four years ago. That's awesome!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: And I looked over at the guy in the co-pilot's seat. He got a big grin on his face, and his thumb up. Because when we were instructing, one of the requirements was to make a steep turn to the left and not lose any altitude and hit your prop wash. In the check flight for graduation, that was one of the assignments: "Give me a steep turn left. I want 360 degrees, and I want you to hit your prop wash." So the student would take the airplane and he passed if he hit his prop wash. And it depended on the rest of his flight that day whether he passed or not, but if he hit that prop wash, he passed regardless of how poorly he flew everything else. That was the key. That meant that he had control of that airplane, he knew where he was, and he had a firm hand on it. That was important to a primary student. He will be successful.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Uh-huh. That's good insight.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Now, I diverted and went backwards, didn't I?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: We're back to.... You said why that was important, because that was a requirement when you were instructing.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Right, when I was checking. We taught it, yes, to our own students, but we checked for it with a check ride. Like I said, back then we had to check each student twice: once at about fifteen hours, and once again just before he graduated. It'd be around fifty, sixty hours, because they had to have sixty hours in primary. They had to fly sixty hours. If they get past the check ride just before they got the sixty hours, they graduated and went on to basic. If they didn't pass it, we could hold them back another class if we thought it would do any good keep them for another thirty days, and work with them some more. Everybody wanted to graduate, because it was a class.... What do you call that when "we're here together, we're all together, let's go together"?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Like a seminar or....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: You're part of something. And they were part of a class, and they did not like to be held back. But we had cadets that got ill and couldn't complete because they had gotten ill. And when they got healthy, we finished them, and they'd go back a class. They'd lose a class, in other words, and go back one. And they hated that! But, you know, "you got sick, I didn't." (chuckles) But anyway, going back to the B-17. I liked the B-17. You could put your feet up on the controls and sit back and relax. You could put your feet up there....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh my gosh! Kind of like an airline pilot, huh? (laughs)

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, they were exposed, you know. The tubes were right there. You could put your feet up on the controls and fly the airplane. Visibility was good. There was no inherent faults with the airplane, like the fuel problem in a B-24. And the B-24 did not have good visibility: it was kind of you were in a crowded cockpit and little tiny windows around. You didn't have good physical vision. So I didn't like the B-24.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: The B-17, you see all those awesome pictures of them coming back with half a wing gone. They were truly afort.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. When you watch TV and you'll see a B-24 wing blow up and (thffftttpppt) fold over the top of the airplane, nobody gets out. You listen to some stories about bailing out the crew, getting everybody out, and the pilot's sitting up there trying to hold the airplane in the sky while he gets everybody out of the airplane, then he has a chance to get out himself. So a lot of times the pilot was left behind. I knew a couple of pilots that ended up bailing out first. Not good. But the panic was there. And they got to that point, "I've got to get out of this thing!" Over the side they go.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Did the rest of the crew get out too, or no?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, he pushed the bell first, and everybody'd head for the exit, (laughs) It depended. The tail gunner didn't usually get out. He had a bail-out problem.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Physically getting out of there?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Uh-huh. But the waist gunner's hatch was right there. He could just abandon. But they usually didn't wear their chute. On my airplane we had two rules: we had a ground inspection before we boarded the airplane. They later did that in the B-29. Crew had to stand there in formation, and the pilot would go down the line and make sure that the harnesses were correct and everything, and brief them as to what the mission was going to be, and what have you. During the 24 and 17 operations, we didn't do that. But I did it. I briefed everybody, made sure they knew what their job position was going to be, and what was going to happen if that bell started ringing. That means, "Don't ask questions. Go!" Anyway, I used to tell them, "When you hear the bell go, just go! because if you get in my way, I'll push you out! I'm coming fast!" (chuckles)

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Now did you have a situation where you had to bail out?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: No, I never had to ring the bell. I was prepared for it, but I never had to ring the bell.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So you just were briefing them on the procedure. Okay.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Uh-huh. Again, I told them to keep their chutes on. If they had a backpack, keep their parachute on. If they had a chest pack, keep it on. And if they didn't agree with me, keep it right in their hand or alongside of them, because you aren't going to have time to grab it if it's someplace else. So the radio operator used to say, "Well, I don't have enough room!" "Ah, you've got enough room. If I've got enough room up there, you've got enough room up there." So [unclear]. Anyway, I had the habit or the procedure of briefing.... They were always students, except for the flight engineer and the pilot and the co-pilot. They were students. They had not graduated, they were cadets. And some of them, of course, had graduated. I shouldn't say they were not.... Some of them were bombardiers learning the mickey. Some of them were navigators learning the rest of the system, and they had graduated. We still had some pilots coming through, learning the system. And so they were commissioned officers. But we had enlisted personnel, aviation cadets, that were learning the system. They weren't in the habit of flying, you might say. It was new to them. Now, it's interesting that when I flew that B-17 about four years ago up at Oshkosh, the guy that was assigned as commander briefed us all. He stood us by the entrance hatch and said what was going to happen, this, that, and the other thing. And he briefed us as to what our responsibilities would or would not be, because they were selling rides to people who had never been in an airplane before. "You can sit here and look out that window, or do that." And when I got out of the seat, because we gave people a chance to sit at the controls, when I got out of the seat I took some of the ladies and took them up in the nose section and showed them how the Norton bomb site worked, because it works, because I knew how to run a bomb site. I did, I learned it [unclear]. I put them in the little seat inside the bomb site, and showed them how to synchronize the thing, and they learned, they learned fast. It's not difficult to do, and it's kind of fun.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Getting up there in that nose would be fun alone!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. Now EAA is not carrying bombs in their airplane. We did. We were carrying bombs. I think the idea there was I'm thinking especially back on it was that the war could get inflamed in a minute's notice. The Japanese could decide to invade the West Coast, was the theory, and they'd have ships and stuff like that to put people ashore. And we were in California, so we flew armed. We had ammo in the guns, we had bombs in the bomb bay, and we had an active bombardier, what have you. So if all of a sudden we got orders, "There's ships out there. Go get 'em and bomb 'em!" we were loaded and ready to go. And maybe you were just flying a training mission and all of sudden you're assigned to go bomb a cruiser or something like that. So we went prepared to go to war. Every day that we flew, we were prepared to go to war. So it was an interesting experience.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So you weren't just doing training you were, that was your primary mission but you had a strong secondary mission, almost like an Air National Guard, prepared to protect.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, prepared to go to physical war.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Uh-huh, because I don't think enough people realize that was a danger, the Japanese might decide.... It's just like what the Germans were doing on the East Coast with the U-boats and things.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Uh-huh. They'd bring their U-boats in back there and start their cannon going.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's right. That's an interesting point, that you weren't just doing the training, that you were really prepared to go to war right then to defend the West Coast.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Right then and there, yeah. We were actively at war on a training mission.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Uh-huh, you were doing both.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: It's kind of like Korea today. The North Koreans and the South Koreans are actively at war. Peace has never happened in Korea. I've been there, I know. When we were in Korea, my wife and I, we took a tour. When John was in Korea John is my son we got picked for a free trip by the Korean government: an indoctrination for in- country families. And we were listed as parents, and so we got selected to come to Korea and take a tour of Korea and learn about Korea. The Koreans were trying to be nice to the United States, to get the United States behind them, and things like that. So we took this tour and we drove up to the DMZ in a bus, and they walked us over to the area where they watch the other side, from our side, and it's like a little fortress with big windows with telescopes and stuff like that, so they can see what the Koreans are doing over there on the north side. And the North Koreans at the DMZ have got a building that's only eight feet deep, but it's about two hundred feet long, at the DMZ contact point. It's where the conferences were held, and we got to go in the building where the conference was held, and there is a line that goes down the middle of the conference table, and a window, and a window, and two flags one North Korean, one South Korean and you're sitting on your side. And the teacher or instructor or guide is on the other side. And you look over at the window, here's a couple of Koreans, got their face right up on the glass, watching what you're doing. And the instructor says, "Now, you notice the two flags, you notice they're both the same size. Well, when we first started this operation, the United States put in a taller flag. So the next day the North Koreans put in a taller flag. So another flag, and another one. The flags were getting too large, so we had to make an agreement so the flags would never get any larger than 'X.' So that's why the two flags are the same size. We had to make an agreement that had to be negotiated." And that's the kind of attitude and atmosphere that exists over there. Everything's up for negotiation. The day before we were there, they had a guy that ran out of the building and ran across the DMZ and wanted sanctuary in the United States.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: It's amazing he got over.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: So they're watching everything. And it's interesting that the building is only eight feet deep, just that office. It's just a long hallway with windows.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Well of course right now we're in a state of war I was just going to make a comment here for the purposes of the tape, that every once in a while we have some airplane noise, the sound of freedom, here at Luke, just to remind us that we're truly here at Luke Air Force Base. Sometimes we might also, if it does get a little loud, you might even want to pick your voice up just a little bit. I'm not sure how much competition we're going to be getting from the airplane noise. I mean, I love the sound of the airplane noise, but it might interfere a little bit.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, if you hear the F-35, it'll get noisier.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: We're thinking positive, we will get the F-35! But anyway, let's go back to our B-17s. I think there was an interesting I'm not sure where this fits in timeline-wise about how you ended up with a police escort going over a certain pass.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah, Cajon Pass.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: What base were you at, where were you going, and why was this happening?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, let's see, April 15, 1945, I met my present wife first one, only one I've ever had I met my wife. She was a student nurse at L.A. County General. Cadet nurses, they called them. She was in the nursing program. And I met her at the Hollywood Palladium, Sunday matinee dance. Want to hear that story?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Sure! Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Okay. My brother and I, who was in the Navy he was a signalman first on the S.S. Simon Benson. The Benson was in Seattle for repairs. They'd been out in the Pac [Pacific Ocean], and he was there in Seattle for repairs. So he got leave, because the ship's not going anyplace for a matter of weeks, so he thumbs his way down to Los Angeles and comes home for several days. We get in my car I'm home we get in my car and we're going to go out to Hollywood to see about some girls. And we're doing Hollywood Boulevard, and we invited a couple of girls into the car. We didn't like them, we told them to get out. Things like that wartime. So after about three of those episodes, we kind of looked at each other, and I said, "You know, this is Sunday afternoon and the Hollywood Palladium has a matinee dance, and there'll be some girls there that would be nice girls, because they come from all over town." And he said "Oh yeah, that's right!" So we went down to the Hollywood Palladium, gave the parking attendant the keys, and he took the car up around to the parking area for the valet parking. We went in and we danced with three or four girls, and then we're standing up on the stair entrance way to the main floor, and we see a couple of cadet nurses over to the side, and I said, "There's a couple of cadet nurses over there. Let's go dance with them." And he said, "Okay." I said, "You do the asking, it's your turn." He said, "No, you get along better with nurses. You do the asking." And I said, "If I do the asking, I do the choosing." And he kind of squinted across the ballroom and he says, "Well, okay, the other one's not so bad." That's an old war-time joke, that the girls always went in twos, one good-looking and one not quite so good-looking, (chuckles) So we went over and I motioned to him, and he did the asking. No, I'm sorry, he motioned at me, and I did the asking. And they both said yes. And so the girl who is now my wife, put out her hand to reach for the sailor, because the only thing she knew was sailors, because all of her classmates were in the Navy. So she's going to dance with the sailor, because she knew what he was. And I was an Air Force lieutenant with a specially-made suit of a pink battle jacket. And all battle jackets were forest green, and mine had been tailor made by my tailor in San Bernardino, and she didn't know what I was. So I just reached out and took her hand. I said, "You're dancing with me." And she looks at Burton, my brother, the sailor that she thought she was going to dance with, and I said, "No, you're dancing with me." Okay, so we danced. And during the dancing session, we kept dancing with them, and we found out that they had to be back at the hospital by ten o'clock. I said, "Well, we'll take you back. You don't have to worry being there, we can get you [there] by ten o'clock." So they thought because they'd always danced with sailors, that [we] were going to take them on the bus, because that's the way the sailors took them back to the hospital. When we get ready to leave to go and they were getting anxious because they didn't think we were leaving enough time to get the bus—anyway, we were headed to where the car exit is, and they wanted to go the other way, because that's where the bus exit is. I said, "We're going this way." She said, "Well, that's the cars out there." And I said, "Well, so, you know, I've got a car." "You've got a car?!" In those days, I had purchased a 1941 Plymouth convertible, black in color, red leather upholstery with a white top, which was down that day. So the black convertible with the red leather upholstery showing, comes whipping around the corner from the parking lot, and pulls up in front of me, and she's just standing there, and I had to take a hold of her, "Come on." She said, "That's your car?!" And I said, "Yes, that's my car." She said, "Ohhh!" (laughter) We still tell the kids that the reason she went with me was I had a car. But we took them back to the hospital, and during the next couple of months I saw her frequently when I was off and could come, and she was going to be off schedule too. I'd drive into Los Angeles from San Bernardino, which was where I was living, flying out of Victorville, and would go over the Cajon Pass every day. So anyway, I'd drive into L.A. and go to the Hollywood Palladium, pick her up at the hospital, and we'd go dancing. So I had taken her back to the hospital one evening, and I was driving back to San Bernardino actually, I was driving to Victorville because I didn't have time to go home, and I was in uniform anyway, so I didn't need a change. I'm driving out Foothill Boulevard, which goes to San Bernardino, and it turns up and goes over Cajon Pass out to Victorville. The air base is just a little ways outside of town. So I'm driving along, and I'm a little bit late, and I had stopped and picked up some air crew from the base at the pick-up station that we had in town free rides for the soldiers. And I'm zipping along, over-fast I'm speeding and all of a sudden there's a red light and a motorcycle alongside of me. So I pull over and this young policeman looks in the window and he says, "Lieutenant, where are you going so fast, what's your hurry?" And I said, "Well, I'm trying to make flight line out at Victorville." And he looks in the back seat and the other side of the front seat, and he said, "Is this your crew?" And I said, "Well, yeah, kind of." And he says, "You goin' to Victorville?" "Yes." "What time is flight line?" And I said, "Five o'clock." "Follow me." So he gets back on his [motorcycle] and turns on his red light and siren, and away we go! He's doing about 90 to 100 miles an hour, up Foothill Boulevard, turns up to go up through the Adelanto Cutoff, and goes up to the freeway, only it wasn't the freeway, it was the Cajon Pass Roadway, and up over the pass, and out into the desert, to where we turned off to go to the base. And he waves me to go by. And so I guess I'd better go by. So I went by, and as I went by, he gave me a salute, and I saluted him back, and went up to the turnoff and turned in and slowed down (chuckles) because I don't like to drive that fast. But anyway, he escorted me all the way from up near Pasadena, to the base. I go in, and I'm way ahead of schedule, so I go to the cafeteria and eat some breakfast. Then I go to the ready room, and I'm sitting there reading, and the guys start coming in. And we'd been passing them all on Cajon Pass, because with the siren going, they're pulling over like they're supposed to, and they know my car, and they know me, and there we go! And they come in there and say, "Where did you get the police escort, and how come?!" and questions like that. And I said, "Well, [unclear] nice and drive your crew out here and give them a free ride, and the cops will be nice to you." (chuckles) So anyway, that was the only time I've had a police escort for a long distance, over a mountain pass, Cajon Pass, and out into the Mojave Desert. I don't want to do it again, but it was a blessing!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: In those days, though, I think my dad has commented too, if you were in uniform, everybody kind of did a little extra for you.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, everybody wanted to be nice to the boys. That was one of the nicest things of being in the service: everybody wanted to be nice to you. Nobody got sassy or mad or anything like that. Nobody cut your line. All those things that people do just because they've got a bad attitude, they didn't do during the war. We get some of that nowadays, incidentally, and the people come up and shake your hand. I had a flight jacket that has a B-17 on the back of it, and people come up to me, "Did you fly B-17s?" "Yes." "I want to congratulate you and thank you."

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's right. Still that good attitude carries on in gratitude.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah, it still goes on today. If I put my jacket on and I really don't wear it anymore if I were to put that jacket on and go to the mall, somebody would talk to me about it.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Sure, absolutely.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: And that's what, fifty years ago?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Longer. Sixty.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Sixty years ago.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Seventy. We're getting up there! It's a long time.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Because the wife and I have been married for sixty-two years. So it was better than sixty years.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's right, more than that.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Because we didn't get married until after the war. I was back in school, and she was graduating from nursing school, and we decided it's the time to do it. So we signed up the Wee Kirk O' the Heather at Forest Lawn and got married.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That was nineteen forty....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, it was sixty-two years ago. What was that, 1946, or something like that?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Something like that, yeah. When you said that your police escort was April '45, that was the month of VE-Day.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yes it was, we were still at war.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah. So you were at Victorville then for VE-Day?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yes. I was on my way from Victorville to Hobbs, New Mexico, because they were getting ready to reassign us the reassignment comes later they were getting ready to reassign us, and I pointed out to Johnny that I was not official or "legal" as we called it, in the B-17, because I had not been to transition. And so he said, "Well, we'll take care of that." So they assigned me to B-17 transition school in Hobbs, New Mexico, where I had to fly a hundred hours, which I did in about thirty days, and qualified that was the word qualified as a B-17 pilot, so that I could accept a different assignment, which means I'm through with B-17s, and I'm through with B-24s, and I'm going to do something else, and I thought maybe I'll finally get my fighter airplane, (chuckles) Yeah, fat chance! So anyway, we were on our way to Hobbs, New Mexico, from Victorville, and we stopped here in Phoenix, in the Hotel Adams, and we had the balcony rooms there were several of us traveling in caravan and we had the balcony rooms at the Hotel Adams, and the Japanese had indicated they were going to surrender, and the United States had dropped a couple of important bombs, and so we were going to accept their surrender, then we wouldn't have to invade them. So the street was closed and full of people. The newspaper had the loudspeakers out and was playing music and giving news broadcasts as to what was going on and what was happening, etc., etc. And the street people turned into dancing because of the music coming over the loudspeaker, so they had this giant street dance going on down below us.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: All the Big Band music, right?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah. Yeah, Big Band Music. You know, Harry James and all of those guys. We were on the balcony, leaning on the balustrades and looking down, you know, "Why don't you come on up?" getting the girls to come up. And we were having our own dance on the balcony. And we had all the ingredients, we had alcohol, because the bell boys would provide it. And so we had a bar, and we were having a good time, everybody was being nice and having fun, just listening for the news, participating in the night, you might say. And then they got the Missouri up to Tokyo so they could hold the ceremony, and they signed off on the treaty, and we had to be at Hobbs the next day. So we took off for Hobbs and went on to Hobbs. But we did celebrate VJ-Day in Phoenix, Arizona, at the Hotel Adams. We had the party of all time at the Hotel Adams! We had food, we had alcohol, we had people, we had music from across the street.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Was there a lot of other military there as well, besides you guys, on that one floor?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well,the balcony was full, because we invited everybody that we thought that looked like they'd like to come up.Katherine Gillen:: But I was just wondering, how much was civilian and how much was military? Was it mostly civilian?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, the girls were all civilians. We didn't really have girl military in those days.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Right, nurses or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: But the guys were probably 95% military enlisted and officers both. We weren't selective.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay. That's cool.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Everybody was buddyin' up.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's cool. It sounds like all downtown Phoenix was a party it wasn't just the hotel.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, yeah, the whole thing. It wasn't the only party in town, incidentally.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah, I just picture this whole.... I'm picturing, you said the streets were blocked off, so I'm picturing everybody dancing and boogying in the middle of the street.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: The other Air Force hotel was about two blocks north of the Adams. It's the one with the tower on, downtown

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay, I know what you mean.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: What's the name of that hotel? Anyway....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Westward Ho?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Westward Ho. The Westward Ho is where if you flew into Phoenix, going to spend a night, so forth and so on, and you're looking for somebody that you know is stationed here, you go to the Westward Ho and sit in the bar. Because if you were stationed here, you would go to the hotel and go in the bar, to see if anybody was looking for you. It was a meeting place. Well, the Hotel Adams was the sleeping place. That was where you stayed, that wasn't where you met people. You stayed at the Adams. Westward Ho was the Air Force meeting place.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Didn't know that!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: I met people there several times. I'd go into the bar, "Oh, hey, there's Jerry!" Go and rap him on the back of his head, (laughter) In fact, even when a person was a cadet here, if they were looking for another cadet, even, or somebody that they thought they would know, they'd go to that hotel, into the bar. If they didn't see anybody they knew, they'd sit for a while. Somebody would come in, maybe another cadet or something like that, and they'd get together, have a couple of drinks, decide what to do. We used to go out to Tempe, because Tempe had a big swimming poolbig swimming pool. So on Sundays we'd go out to Tempe to the swimming pool, and they'd let us in free, incidentally.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Of course!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: And it was a beautiful pool set-up. It's not there anymore, but it was a beautiful pool set-up, had high-dive bars, and I used to dive, and just go swimming, spend the afternoon.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's quite a trek across town, getting over to Tempe.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, it was about twenty-some odd miles. Well, heck, it was twenty-six miles from here at Luke, into town.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: And it was nothing....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: How many of the roads were even paved back then?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, this one out of here, going to Glendale, was paved. And you got to Glendale, made a 3 5-degree turn to the right, and go down to what was [Highway] 60 even then it was 60 and it'd take you right into town.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay, so that was all paved.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: That was another twelve miles.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: So we'd do that all the time.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So you guys were hanging out there at the Westward Ho and everything. Here on base at the time, was there really anything that was close to being a club? Or was it just a chow hall? Was there like an "O" club or an enlisted club or anything like that here on base?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: On the air base?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Here at Luke.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, there was an officers club here. If we got permission, we could participate there. But there was an enlisted club here too. But we really didn't have time to get active in either one of those, because town was right over there, and we'd go to town. You don't even have an officers club anymore.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: It's just one club nowadays. Yeah, the last year it formally went to one club.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Combined them. Air Force wives activity. GlLLEN: Well, Navy and Army too, they're all kind of doing that now.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: You know, I'm going to have to excuse myself and go across the hall. I've got orders to remember. I'm on a two-hour shift.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay. Well, we are still at about, what are we, an hour and a half?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, at least an hour and a half.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So let me go ahead and make sure I can....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, no, it's two and a half hours, because we started at nine o'clock.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: No, we started at ten.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, ten? Oh, okay. If you don't mind breaking.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: I don't mind. (aside about son's recorder, narrator exits, recording paused)

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay, we were talking about VJ-Day and the Adams Hotel. It sounds like you had an awesome time. Did anybody sleep? Or the next morning you had to go to Hobbs, you said.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Eventually it broke up.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: About what time of the morning did you start driving for Hobbs, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: I don't know. It was very early. It wasn't very far before dawn, because I remember the sun came up over there. Katherine Gillen:: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: From here to Hobbs is quite a drive.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah. You've got to go all the way across the rest of Arizona, and about two- thirds of [New Mexico], because Hobbs is almost over to the Texas border.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah, New Mexico, that's quite a ways.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: In fact, while we were at Hobbs, they used to hire us to run booze over to Texas, because right next door to Hobbs was a dry county, and they knew that the police wouldn't molest or stop or anything, a military....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So there was a dry county in Texas?!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah, right next door.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh my goodness!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: You'd pull into this wholesaler place, and they'd throw some stuff in your trunk, and give you some money, and an address where to take it, and you'd drive it over to Texas and pull into this place and pop the trunk open, and they'd take the cases out, and then you'd turn around and go back. You'd already been paid.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: (laughs) Did the commanding officer know about this, or was this something that was just kind of like....Dale Huss:: I don't know whether Nisley [phonetic] knew about it or not. The commanding officer here was Colonel Nisley.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: At Hobbs?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Nisley was here, and he was in control of us at Hobbs.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh! Really?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: We were on duty at Hobbs from here.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh,that's.... Even....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, I'm sorry, from at....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Victorville?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Victorville, [unclear].

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay, so he was in charge having....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: I don't know the commanding officer of Victorville. I met him a couple of times, but I don't remember his name. He was a nice guy. He didn't give us any trouble. But we got our orders changed there to get out of that training session that we were in, and go back to flying. He was nice about it. I think he helped do it. I think he disagreed with the fact that highly-trained pilots were being wasted. And that's what it was, was a waste.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah. So you did get to Hobbs, though.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, and flew the B-17 another hundred hours, in a matter of a few weeks. And then we went from there to Texas for our next assignment, and I found out that my next assignment was a B-29. And that's when I told the Air Force, "No, I'm a fighter pilot, trained at Luke Field, and I'm not going to fly B-29s. What do I have to do to go home? War's over, I'll go home." I was very disenchanted with the Air Force at that time. I had been wasted, as far as I was concerned. "Where do I sign? What do I do?" And he turned the paper around and said, "Lieutenant, you sign right there." I'm refusing an order, and that was how you got out of active duty in the Air Force in those days. After the war, refuse a direct order, and you're done. They don't need you, they're glad to see you go. They don't have to pay you when you go, because they didn't pay the reservists. They transferred us to the reserve, those that refused to take that 29 assignment, they transferred us to the active reserves, and eventually the inactive reserves, which they had nothing going for them at the end of the war, they had to get organized. Well, the 452nd Bomb Group, which had been in England, based in southern England, and flew Germany, so forth and so on, was assigned to be at Long Beach, California. So I got assigned to the 452nd Bomb Group, and reported in to Long Beach, where I was assigned as an instructor pilot, because I had been an instructor pilot the whole time, and I was flying T-6s, and T-l Is, and an occasional DC-3 type flight. Some lieutenant colonel busted our TC-3 when he tried to land at Chanute Air Force Base in the winter, (laughs) Hit a building! Destroyed the building, destroyed the airplane, destroyed half of the passengers, and they were all guys hitchin' a free ride to Chicago. So no more DC-3. They brought a C-74 in there one oh, I guess it was there for about a week, and we all got an orientation ride in a C-74. I said, "I'm glad I'm not flying one of these!" Because in those days, it was before they built a new cockpit over the top of the fuselage, and you sat in a blister. You know what a C-74 is?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: I've probably seen a picture of it.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: It's a giant, four-engine transport.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Really I'm picturing something huge.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah, big four-engine transport. A great big fuselage cargo carrier. And it had a fighter-type cockpit on it. So you sit in the cockpit at the controls, and you've got to do this, to see the instrument panel. You cannot see it from the pilot's seat. You've got to get down and look underneath the fuselage to see the instrument panel. And I'm saying, "Now these kind of airplanes fly a lot of instruments. How the devil do they fly instruments when they've got to get out of shape to even see them?!" So I was glad they didn't assign the 452nd to C-74s. That's why it was there, was to determine whether that would be the next assignment, for C-74s, made by Douglas.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: I just want to say, for clarification purposes, because you went to the active reserves, was that the 452nd right then?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: That's the 452nd based at Long Beach, California.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay, so you left Texas, went home, said goodbye.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Went back to school.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's right. Let's talk about that. You decided to go back, and the first school you went to....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Was USC, and I was assigned to that's not the right word to use now.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: You signed up.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Anyway, my first class was an English class in Bovart [phonetic] Auditorium, which is a humongous auditorium. It's intent is to hold the whole student body. Okay, USC's not a small school. So I'm in this thing, and there had to be hundreds of G.I.s, fresh out of the service, having to attend this class as their first class at USC, and it's November of 1945.
