And I'm sitting there and this lecturer, professor, is up there lecturing away and drawing things on a giant blackboard, and things like that, and I said "This is not my next four years. I'm not going to do this for four years." Too many ex- G.I.s here at S.C. It's a big school, and it's a very noteworthy school, and a very desirable school. I grew up in southern California, I've been an S.C. fan since I was a kid. My brother went to S.C. before the war. He left after two years, because he wanted to be in the Navy. Worst decision he ever made. But anyway, I went home and I said, "I'm not going to go to USC." And my mother said, "Well, what are you going to do?" And I didn't tell you this, I said, "I'm going to go out to Cal R. Tech, and see what's going on there." Because Major C. C. Mosley [phonetic] owns it and is running it. He was the head of Cal Aero at Chino, which is a big air operation now, Confederate Air Force type operation now. C. C. Mosley owned Glendale Airport when I was working there. "And so I'll go out there." So I went out and talked, and, "We'll start you tomorrow." It was a two-year engineering for mechanical engineers for the aircraft industry. That's the only goal we had, the only goal we were given. We were not going to be teachers or professors or anything like that. We were going to be design engineers for the aircraft industry which needed us very drastically. While I was in school, I was offered a job at North American, but they wanted me to be an electrical wiring diagram designer, and I didn't want to do that. So I went over to Northrop and showed them my project book, an airplane I designed, which would fall into the EAA nowadays as a home-built type aircraft. It was a [unclear] airplane with a rotary, you know, a round engine in it. Every airplane has to have a round engine the B-17, B-24, all got round engines all except that P-51. But anyway, it had a round engine on it, which was made by Ken Royce, which was a pretty good engine maker back before the war. And I was going to use one of Ken's engines. So the engineering director kept my project book and said they'd let me know if they were interested. So I went home, left my book there. It was everything you needed to build that airplane: all the drawings and the whole bit, to build that airplane, complete. And I went home. And I no sooner got there and had changed clothes, because I was building a house, and the phone rings. So I answered the phone. It's Northrop. They want me to come to work tomorrow! Well, they wanted me to come to work that afternoon, really, and I said, "No, I've already gotten home." And I lived twenty miles away in Glendale. And I said, "I've already gotten home and changed my clothes, and I'm working on the house that I'm building. I can come tomorrow." "Okay, we'll see you tomorrow." So I went down there to hire in, and I started working. I didn't hire in, I was put to work! They got their information, gave me a drafting board and a drafting machine. "Here, this is what we need." That afternoon I'm driving the machine to draft parts for them, for the XP-89.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Tell me about that plane. I'm not real familiar with that.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, XP-89.... Northrop, you know, during the war built the PC-61, the night fighter, the Cobra. Anyway, it was a twin engine night fighter, black in color, guns all over, a radar set in the back end. It was the only airplane really credited with shooting down any night airplanes, because it could see them, and they couldn't see it. In fact, our vice-president even flew one overseas as a demonstration and shot down an airplane. He was a civilian, and he shot down a Zero.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Wow!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: It's been hush-hush ever since, because it was illegal, so don't put....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Well, I don't think anybody's going to haul him away at this point.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: So towards the end of the war the war wasn't really over they gave Northrop a contract to build the XP back when all fighters were "P's" 89, which was a night fighter, a twin engine night fighter, jet. Big thing, 20,000 pounds, black in color, cannons coming out of the nose four of them. We called it the "gun nose." And Hughes built the gun nose for us Hughes Aircraft over in Culver City. And I designed the bulkhead that nose was to fasten onto. So I had to coordinate with Hughes Aircraft, and so I met Howard Hughes.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Did you really?!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: As in not just shake his hand, but talk to him for a while?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: He came into a conference that I was in.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: What was your impression of him?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Nice guy.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Really loved aviation. Did you see the movie, "The Aviator"?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: I don't think I quite realized how much of an aviator he was at heart.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: That's how he got started. He did that for fun. He made his money making drills for the oil wells, but he flew airplanes for fun,

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: At heart he was an aviator and built airplanes, racing planes and things like that. He was a real flyer. He was a real character too. But we were in this conference, discussing things that you do in conferences, and this guy comes into the room, and I look and say, "That's Howard! I've seen him at Glendale. That's Howard." He sits down in an empty chair and listens, and then he asks some questions and everything. And then he told the Northrop people, which I was one that was there, that if he can do anything for us on this project, to let him personally know. We never needed to, because we got all kinds of cooperation. You know, the boss is standing there saying, "If you need anything, you see me." They're going to make sure that we don't need anything, they don't want us to see him. So anyway, he was in the conference room a while, and then he left tennis shoes and all. And you know, people didn't wear tennis shoes in those days. Howard did tennis shoes and all. I've been on the [Spruce] Goose.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh, you were?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah. I was out in the hangar while they were building it. We'd go over to Hughes to do some business, and then go out in the hangar while we were there.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Huge.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. Go on board. When it was down in Long Beach, I was on board. I took Faye, took my wife, and they had a fantastic display of the thing down there. And so we went down to see the Goose, and you get to go through the Goose. I sat in the pilot's seat. This is a beautiful airplane. There's all kinds of room in that cockpit. Big windows. Of course the airplane was huge, but big windows, and a nice instrument panel. Controls where they belonged. You could move the controls. You weren't flying, so you didn't know what they would do when you put some air on 'em, but you could move the controls. Nice, nice system. And six engines out that way, and six engines out that way. Crazy! But anyway, yeah, I met Howard, and I liked Howard. He was nice. He was nice to us, and I liked [being nice too?]. But anyway, I designed the bulkhead that nose bolted to. And I designed that bomb pedestal for the XP-89, I told you about yesterday. Then I got into controls design, and designed the fly-by-wire controls or helped design, I didn't do the whole thing helped design the fly-by-wire system for the XF-4, which's sole purpose in being was to develop fly-by-wire controls. And the XF-4 was the little tiny flying wing that we used to develop it. We hired Charlie Tucker, who was a race pilot, to fly it, because he was the only pilot with enough skill, that was small enough to get into the thing. It was tight! I got into it one time in the hangar while we were building it, and sat there. I thought, "Man! there ain't no room in this thing!" (laughter) You know, [I'm] used to B-17s and B-29s and B-24s, and [here I was] in this little XF-4.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Now explain the importance of that fly-by-wire system that you worked on so much.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Fly-by-wire is where you control the airplane by wire, electrical system. You've got a sensor box that you tell the servos out at the controls what to do, how to move the control system: the elevators and the rudder, so forth and so on, the ailerons. There is no direct linkage.... All airplanes had cables or rods going to the controls from the [unclear]. And you had a stick in the middle like in a single-engine airplane you've got a stick in the middle, and you move it that way, and the rods out on the end push the elevators. You move it over here, and the rods that go out through the wing push the ailerons. That's the normal control system, and we're still building airplanes that way. How many years has it been? (laughs) But Eads [phonetic], the French company, got into the fly-by-wire system, which they bought from Northrop. It controls the airplane without direct control that's the best way to say it. You aren't touching them, you're sending them a signal, an electronic signal, to do something. The little box like you've got in your F-16 out here, is the box that has all the electronics in it, that's on the wire, and it's not cable, it's a wire, like an electrical wire in a house, only much smaller than that. And it sends a signal out that wire to do something out there with that aileron, make it go this way or that way.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So a totally different way of controlling the plane.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Of controlling it. Now, I can't remember his name, put that airplane down on the Hudson, he lauded his success because of the fly-by-wire system that airplane had. He did not have any trouble controlling the airplane on his final approach without any power.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: [Chesley] "Sully" Sullenberger? He had a little bit of electrical power that could read his signals and tell the controls what to do, so he could keep the airplane level and get the nose up to impact the water, and things like that. Fly by wire.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And that's the system that you started working on, started there at Northrop.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yup. I was working in the controls department as a designer, and the guy that invented the system was the supervisor. And he assigned me to work on that little box of electronic controlswith the joy stick, as we call a stick in an airplane with the joy stick on the top of it. You had an arm rest, and you grabbed that thing and you just (fswip, fswip, fswip) do anything. Charlie Tucker, famous person, didn't like our XF-4, because he didn't think it would go fast enough. He couldn't get it to go fast enough to suit him. And I would like to tell him, it wasn't designed to go fast, it was designed to control the airplane precisely, without direct contact.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And that was an Air Force contract, anyway, wasn't it? You said that's what they wanted.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yes. Well, Charlie worked for us for a while. After he got out of the Air Force, he came to work for Northrop.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: But you were doing what the Air Force asked you to do in the contract, right, by designing it that way?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. The supervisor had the design plan. He invented the system, you might say. And we were assigned as mechanical engineers, to do it and make it work. I only had so much space for that box, and I had to get all that junk inside of the thing. And I had to have clearance to move them, because you've got to have something send the signal to the relay that sends the signal out to the wing or to the tail or there's no tail on the XF-4 out to the back end. [unclear] there's a rudder, but there's no tail.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah. So it wasn't designed to go supersonic, that particular plane.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: No. But you see, the world was fascinated with supersonic airplanes. You've got a couple of them parked in the parking lot up here. They don't fly by wire, though. (chuckles) So anyway, it was being designed, developed, and originated at Northrop as a project, and I got to work on it.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: How many years were you with Northrop?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Forty years.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Wow. Good company to work for?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah! Great company. Jack Northrop, a prince.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Saw lots of changes in aviation, too, in that period.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah. We built the flying wings, the B-49, for example. I did some work on a B-49. I did some work on the YC-125, which was a three-engine cargo airplane. What I did there was I hung the JATO bottles on the landing gear in order to help get the airplane off the ground. I was a mechanical engineer, so I did mechanical design. The B-49, ha!, we installed a radar system in the B-49. Guess who got to design and install every new system? (laughs) It doesn't pay to have work experience. They'll grab ya'.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Installing radar systems.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: "You know about radar...." And they gave me all of the poop sheets. Okay, I know that system, I've worked on that system, I've flown that system. And I had a special area in the middle section of the B-49 that's the big flying wing in the middle section, to put it in, with an operator to operate it. When you installed it, it never operated on the airplane in flying. They never flew it, in other words. So I don't know if it worked or not it should have.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So you were always kind of still touching base with the Air Force with all these different contracts, obviously, but there was a little story about how you really parted ways with the reserves Korea?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, well, yeah. Like I said, I was now in the active reserve, flying as an instructor pilot for the 452nd Bomb Group. Well, the 452nd got picked up at the beginning of Korea and was assigned to go to Korea. Well, we had two squadrons on Long Beach....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And what were you flying?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: T-6s, T-l Is, and that's basically it.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: But what were you going to fly if you went to Korea?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: They changed them to B-26s, which is an airplane I volunteered to fly at the end of the war, and didn't get the assignment. The B-26 was a Douglas Invader. It's a beautiful airplane. The guy that made ball point pens used to fly them around the world at high speed he and Paul Manson [phonetic] and people like that. But it was a big twin-engine Douglas airplane, nice airplane, beautiful design a dream to fly, according to the pilots and I didn't get picked. But anyway, the 452nd got assigned to B-26s, and they got sent up the valley I think it was at Fresno where they checked them out and flew them over to Korea. They could make that flight landed a couple of times, but they could fly as far as Korea, and they did. And then they promptly forgot them over there, and left them over there, and left them over there. And only recently, I think it was the last two years, Air Force Magazine did an article about that bomb group and those airplanes and the job that they did, and even mentioned how they got left over there. And again, the pilots all wrote their congressmen, and got pulled back. It does work to write your congressman!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah, that's what they're there for.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: But anyway, I would have had to go to Korea, because I would have wanted to, to fly that airplane. But I wasn't going to go to Korea, fly any airplanes we had at the 452nd. And so three of us instructor pilots, who all were supervisors at Northrop all three of us were supervisors at Northrop we all knew each other real well, of course, because of our reserve assignment. And so we knew each other well at Northrop. One was in Controls, and I knew him very well, because we worked together. One was what the hell was Sammy doing? Structures, he was doing structures. Yeah. I forgot what the other guy was doing. But anyway, we all went in to see yesterday I called him a colonel, but he was a general, he was a B.G. anyway, we went in to see him. He was the commanding officer of the 452nd. And I'm doing the talking, and I told him that I was not going to go to Korea willingly because I had a family and I worked at Northrop in a very important job, I was management personnel there, and I'm quite sure that the company would not release me. And I told him, "If you'd like a letter from Jack Northrop that tells you that, I'll get you one." I knew Jack! That's a famous phrase. Now it's a dirty phrase, but it used to be a famous phrase, "I know Jack!" But anyway, I knew Jack and I said, "I'll get a letter from him if you'd like one." Well, the general said, "No, that won't be necessary, because I think I can get along without...." And the first guy said, "Me too!" The second guy, "Me too!" You know, when I said, "...get a letter from Jack Northrop," [they all said] "Me too!" "Me too!" So he said, "I can get along without all three of you, because we're going to be doing something different, and I won't need you, so I'll write paperwork to release you to the inactive reserve," which he did. So we stayed at Northrop, and went to the inactive reserve, which meant we went to a class every month in a Northrop building, incidentally and learned all about how the Air Force does things, (chuckles) Just like teaching us to be a soldier, (laughs) We were already a soldier long past.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah, you already knew how the Air Force did things!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: And because of the credits I got by going to that class, the Air Force finally, after all that time, promoted me to first lieutenant. And the lieutenant colonel that was running the class, who was also a Northrop employee, but not a member of the 452nd, he handed me my orders that promoted me, and he says, "Now I guess we won't be seeing very much of you, will we?" I said, "You won't be seeing me at all, because this is the only reason I was here." After all this time I've been working for this, and I've got it, and I'm through. I said, "I quit the Air Force." And I did, I quit the Air Force. I was mad. Then I raised a son that's a colonel in the Air Force! We're very proud of John. Gillen : Well, it must have been really great for you to be able to come back here to Luke at different times when he's been here either for training or in command and different positions.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. His mother always blames me for getting him in the Air Force, (laughs)

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Well, you have some new good memories here.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, I know I paid for his flying lessons when he was in high school. And incidentally they were fairly cheap, because I earned the money by doing jury duty in Chicago. The government selected me for jury duty in the federal courts, and I was there for a couple of months, and they paid fairly good. And I took all that money and gave it to him and I said, "Go buy yourself some flying lessons." So he was already flying with a license when he came to the academy in 1980 graduated in '84.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And then when you retired from Northrop, at some point you decide that you wanted to come back to Arizona again.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, no, we went to California. When I retired from Northrop, we went back to California. We had transferred to our division in Chicago. We were at Rolling Meadows on Hicks Road. That's the Defense Systems Division. It's part of the Electronics Division.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: So you went from California to Illinois; Illinois to California; and then decided that maybe Arizona would be a good place to come back to.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, yeah, we were living in northern California, up in the mountains, and we just decided it would be nice to be in Arizona, because he was here. Our daughter was here. The kids got together and decided we had to go and live in an area where one of them was, that we had to have some supervision. Our oldest daughter, who is an R.N. and teaches, lives in southern Illinois, because she married a boy from southern Illinois, and she was going to a mid Illinois college. Okay? And we decided we did not want to live in southern Illinois no way. I was offered a lot on the lake, that they owned the development. Larry's father suggested maybe I'd like to build a place on a lake and so forth. No sir! Don't want to do that. And the only way to do that gently, is to move back to California when I retire, to get out of town, so I'm not in northern Illinois, so I can't blame the weather. I can blame the weather by moving to California, but I can't blame the weather for moving to southern Illinois, because it's just as bad down there as it is in northern Illinois. So anyway, we moved back to California. John, at that time, was in Italy, I think. I think he was in Aviano. But anyway, he was overseas. And Holly, of course, lives here. And Holly's not married, and the other two are. So we said, "Okay, we'll move back to Phoenix," because we liked it here. We both liked it here. We'd been in and out as snowbirds for years. And we RV'ed for years after I retired. We didn't move anyplace, we just RV'ed. Actually, we bought a place in California that we could park the RV when we weren't using it, and then we RV'ed from there. We'd come here, spend some winter months. Then we'd go around through the South and do all the battlefields up through Gettysburg and around, and over to EAA and spend a month there. We worked at EAA. Convention lasts a week, and we worked the three weeks in front, and the one week afterwards. We had to help set the conference up, and take it down after it was over. So we like Wisconsin, we liked that. That's a good time of year in Wisconsin. So we liked that function, because I was involved with the flight line. What I did for EAA was to drive a transit train between the campgrounds, far distance out, down to the flight line where the volunteers worked. They'd go out on the line and park airplanes. Hundreds of airplanes come in there, and they'd park airplanes. I did that a couple of times. It's a hard-workin' job. I got the job of driving the tram, and they gave me the job of organizing the trams. So I had to figure out the schedule, get the volunteers to drive them, and things like that, plan the route that they're going to drive because it changed. As they kept moving the grounds around and doing things, we had to move the trams. We used to go down the flight line, and we had to quit doing that because we got in the way of the P-51 s. (laughter) P-51 s were all lined up to take off and do their show one day, and I had to go down that line, and I went right behind the P-5 Is, because they weren't ready to go, they hadn't been cleared to take off. They were all sitting there, all herringboned out, with their engines turning. And I went down the line behind them. The next day I hear from my boss that we've got to quit going down the line somebody from the P-5 Is complained. So okay, we'll move in more. Then I had to go through the people traffic. So then we had to change that, because we couldn't run over the people. We'd drive a John Deere tractor and pull two trams that John Deere used to go around through their factories with their tours. They'd lend them to us every year. And I had three trams, three Caterpillar tractors pulling trams.Katherine Gillen:: Are you still active with EAA?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: No, I'm not even a member anymore.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay. Your life has truly been an aviation life, though. Ever since you were a child, in various ways, whether it was the Air Corps, the Air Force, designing planes.... I know you kept your hand in flying planes of different types over the years.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, I owned an airplane, gave that a try. Had to give it up because it costs too much. Us civilians can't afford that.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: That's right! (chuckles) But as we kind of round things out, if there are any other memories you'd like to record, that would be great. There was one kind of image you left me when we were talking before, though, and it goes back to the war: When you were driving near Hobbs one night, and then suddenly you saw....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh, the explosion, yeah.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah, and what your thoughts were at the time.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: My thought was, "They've done it!"

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Well, let's go back what did you see? This was the first experimental....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: I saw the whitest [unclear] cloud, light burst. It's like they talk about when you see Jesus, you see a white light. But I saw that giant white light, power.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: The first "A" bomb.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, it was the first atomic explosion. It was out there at White Sands, near Roswell. They had it on a tower, and they blew it at a hundred feet of altitude, and it just went (wishhh!).

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And you were like 200-300 miles away, but you saw it.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: I've never seen anything else like it.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And you also knew then....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: ...what it was, because in Victorville we were training people that were going to drop those bombs. And so we were working with the pattern of what they were trying to develop. We knew what the bomb was all about. We knew what would happen if they ever exploded one. And when I saw that thing, my only thought was, "They've done it!" You recognized success, and this time it was success in the sky. They'd done it! War's over!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: War's over. Yeah, you knew.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Oh yeah! Drop that thing on them, and they'll quit. And that's what happened. They dropped the one, and Baxter went over with the second one the next day, and dropped it on the other town. We didn't have to drop any more, we didn't have to hit the other three towns that were set for it, because there were five towns and I don't think you should put this in the report but there were five towns that had been selected to test the bomb. When they got the bomb, that's where they were going to test the bomb. The other three got to stay pure, because the first two caused the war to stop. The Japanese [said], "We quit! You're killing too many people!" And those are ancillary people, those are not soldiers or anything like that. But they could see what was going to happen if we kept flying out of Okinawa and not just dropping regular bombs on Tokyo they were going to drop one of those things someplace else, and someplace else, and someplace else, and eventually we're going to drop one on Tokyo, and we'll get Tojo, we'll get the Prince of Power, we'll kill everybody. It's very impressive.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah, must have been an amazing sight to see. And since you knew what they were working on, and you were helping train for that anyway, you knew that was it.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. And when the bomb went down on Hiroshima, and we got the report, I said, "Okay, now the war is over." It was about ten days later that the Japs decided to quit, because Baxter had to drop one on....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Nagasaki.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: But anyway, it's a very impressive thing.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Is there anything that we haven't covered that you'd like to talk about? Anything dealing especially with any flying memories? I'm sure there's a lot of little things we could add into it. We could probably do another two hours, but I was just wondering if there was any major.... We covered pretty much everything that....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: It's like when we owned the airplane, and we swallowed the valve over the Pacific Ocean, and I had to land downwind between the two runways at Santa Monica. It was pretty much the end of my flying career. My mother-in-law had to pick us up at the airport, because we had to leave the airplane at Santa Monica.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: This was you and your wife were flying in what plane was it?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: My wife was just about ready to check out and solo the airplane.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: And what plane was this again?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: My Fairchild 24. She was just about ready to become a pilot. She was learning, and I was doing a pretty good job of teaching her, and she was doing a darned good job of learning. She was never confident, but when that valve got swallowed, and we made that forced landing, oh, I mean the airplane was smoking like crazy because the oil was being burned up, and this, that, and the other thing. And I'm calling "May Day!" to get the tower to clear the pattern and what have you, and they didn't answer me, they didn't come on. And I'm on the emergency frequency, and I'm May Day'ing it, and nothing. And so I landed and the tower calls me and says, "Where did you come from?!" I said, "I came from out over the ocean, but where were you when I was trying to call you with a May Day call?!" He said, "Well, you're transmitting [on] 12-14," or some dumb thing like that, which is the emergency frequency. He said, "You're transmitting on that frequency, and we've got so much VHF" VHF was brand new "we've got so much VHF traffic here, that we don't guard that frequency anymore." And I told him, "That is the national emergency frequency. You either guard it starting now, or I will report this incident to the FAA. Do you want me to do that?" "No, I'll turn it up." (laughs) Geez! He's sitting on a major airport in a control tower and he's not guarding the emergency frequency, because he's got so much VHF traffic. I didn't have VHF. My airplane was an antique, it was a 1939 airplane. I had radio, and a loop antenna for navigation, all that kind of stuff. I had a big round engine up there, 160 horsepower.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Well, I'm so glad that you and your wife made it back.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: So were we! (laughter) It was pretty much the end.... I bought a new engine and we hung it, and then I sold the airplane. My mechanic was extremely disappointed, because previously he had swallowed a valve, and we'd replaced a cylinder head replaced the whole cylinder. And then I'm flying up to my sister's place up at Oxnard, and we were shortcutting across Dana Point coming home, which brings me out over the ocean towards Catalina, to go down before I turn into Torrance, which was where I was basing my airplane. Torrance during the war was a B-24 base, incidentally. And I was parking in a B-24 revetment. Owned my own, nobody else in there, (aside about tissue) But anyway, we were out there, we had just come over Dana Point. Are you familiar with the Los Angeles area?

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: In general. I've been there a few times.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: We'd just come over Dana Point, when "bang!" the engine went. Santa Monica's over there. So I told my wife, "We're going to have to land. If I have to land on the beach, this is what you do, because the airplane will probably turn over. If I have to land on the water because there's too many people on the beach" it was a Sunday afternoon "the airplane will definitely turn over." Fixed gear, okay? "It will definitely turn over. Just before we get to where we touch down, you will unlatch the door so it will open easily" they're like automobile doors on those sort of things" and after I touch down, you get out of the airplane as fast as you can, any way you can. Don't stay with the airplane, get out. Even if we're in the water, get out!" So then we're going, and I'm going down and down and down, and I said, "Now, I think I can make Santa Monica, but there's a big boulevard that goes into Santa Monica there. If I can't make it, I'll land on the boulevard, and we'll probably hit a car or something like that. But if I can make it to the airport, we're going to have to land downwind, because I can't get the tower to stop the traffic, and I've got to get between whatever traffic they have." So we made it just across the approach of the runway and landed on the mat that's paved between the two runways. The runways went like this, and this was a paved mat. So we came this way, right over the end of the airport, "boom!" onto the mat, slammed on the brakes, stopped the airplane, right in the middle of the mat. I'm sitting out there, and it's going like this because of the smoke that's coming out of the cowling. I said, "Get out! Get out!" So she went out the door, and I went out, and as I'm talking to the tower from outside, "Where were you?!" Oh, that was bad!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Well, they weren't sending out fire engines or anything like that?! Nothing?!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh my gosh!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: They asked me, "Are you in a fire?" I said, "No, we've swallowed a valve, and that's just the oil." And he said, "Well, do you need a tow?" I said, "It won't run this way." So they sent a line cart out to tow me in. They towed me in to a fixed base operator, and I made a contract with him to install the engine when I could get one. So he parked the airplane in his hangar, and then I got on the horn to well, oddly enough, it was the guy that owned the engine franchise in Glendale. And I talked to him and he said, "Well, I've got an engine that during the war was hung on a blimp. It's a very good engine in excellent condition. You can have it for a reasonable price if you'd like it." And I said, "I'll take it, but it needs to be delivered to Santa Monica," and I told him the name of the guy that had my airplane. He said, "Oh yeah, I know him, I've delivered engines to him before. I'll send it out." So he sent me an engine to replace my engine. He got the old engine, which I'm quite sure he rebuilt. But I just happened to know that they were on Glendale [unclear] Glendale. I know my way around you! He was right next door to Tim.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Well, I think we're well into lunchtime. I think again your son's probably wondering what's happening. But we've had a lot of good memories. I really thank you for your time, above all, and your memories, and your service to your country. That's the very big thing, is your service to your country.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Well, I didn't serve my country in combat.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: But you served your country in many ways, and all the training you did.... My father served in World War II, in the medical corps in England. He said, "Well, I wasn't in combat." I said, "You saved a lot of lives." So there's a lot of aspects to being in a war. It's not just being out there in the trenches, literally. There's a lot of ways you can serve your country [unclear].

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: In a lot of ways I was very fortunate that I wasn't in combat, because I probably would have got my you-know-what shot off!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: I don't know, I think you were a pretty darned good pilot, from what I can tell!

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: You got on a bomb run in a B-24 or a B-17, you don't get to pilot, you just drive a right straight line, because you're flying on him, and you're flying on him, and he's flying on them, and there's [unclear] guys behind you, and you're all going just like this, to the pattern, you might say, and they're (pock! pock! pock! pock! pock! pock! pock!) letting it have [i.e., the enemy is using anti-aircraft bombardment]. Combat is not a place to be in a bomber. When I was going through cadets, I made that statement, "I do not want to fly a bomber." Because we were asked to volunteer, identify what we wanted to fly. I used to tell my cadet students, "Fly a fighter. Don't fly a bomber. A bomber is nothing but a great big truck that's hauling a lot of explosives, and you can get blown up. Be a fighter pilot and fly a fighter airplane." In those days, they were building P-51 s down in southern California. "Get yourself assigned to a P-51. That's an airplane. Fly that." That's what my Number One student got, incidentally. He went from here to P-5 Is. My comrades here all went to P-39s out at the desert. Me....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Well, you just don't know why....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: But you know, once you get assigned to the training command, especially as an instructor, you're assigned, you're an instructor. They've got an investment in you, that you teach, so you teach.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: You said how much you liked instructing, so I think that came out a lot. So I think that probably had a lot to do with it.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I didn't like instructing in bombers, but I liked instructing in little airplanes. I bought a Fairchild because it flies like a T-6. They don't build them anymore, but they're still available. Get a trainer plane, you'll always find a couple of Fairchilds in there. I had a guy really work on me at Oshkosh one time, trying to sell me a Fairchild, and I said, "No, I had one, and I'm not going to buy another one." And he's out there banging on the fabric with his hands, "This is recent cover. It is solid!" (wham! wham!) And I said, "It won't be for very long!" (laughs)

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: I think you would have found yourself at home here with all the training that goes on in single-seat aircraft here. So it's really a blessing that your son is an F-16 pilot. It all came out in the wash, as they say.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: I got to fly the flight simulator on the A-10, when he was flying A-10s. And I got to fly the flight simulator on the....

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: F-15. Gillen : Fifteen, did you do that as well?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Sixteen. I didn't do the 15.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Okay, because we had 15s here for a while.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: On the F-16, I was flying along, and I'm going to refuel, so I'm going to fly up and get the nozzle in, so forth and so on. Wiped the nozzle right off the airplane! (laughter)

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Well, that's a tricky thing to do. I mean, I was in the simulator too, and I didn't even bother doing that kind of thing, and I was terrible. But they wanted me to see what it was like, so it was very cool. Yeah, it was very cool.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, I felt very lucky that he got me into the thing.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah, the F-16 is an awesome airplane, that is for sure. We've had a lot of the noise of it here, so I'm not sure how much is actually going to show up on the taping, but that's the sound of freedom here.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Yeah. We got up in the new tower, talked to the guys up there. What a fantastic operation!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Oh yeah, very much so.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: That's the day that John's boss, the colonel can't think of his name, going to have lunch with him today.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Colonel Wright?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: But anyway, he and the brand-new general that was going to be commanding officer he didn't have his stars yet, but....

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: General Jones maybe?

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: Jones, yeah. He'd been nominated, but he hadn't been pinned yet. So they came in, they'd been in Texas. They came in and landed, and I'm up in the tower when they landed, watching the guys bring them in, put them in the pattern and bring them down, and they both landed in formation. Beautiful!

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: It's awesome, yeah. Luke is an awesome place. We're blessed to be apart of it. I love working here, so I know what you mean. Every day is....Great place.

sp.speaker: Dale Huss
sp.p: I asked John this morning if he misses the flying end of it, because he doesn't get to fly anymore, and he said, "Not really. I've done it. I'm getting to where I'm not good enough at it to keep doing it. There's other people who can do it better." So he's not doing it anymore.

sp.speaker: Katherine Gillen
sp.p: Yeah. Just even being around them is awesome. All right. Well, thank you kindly. Thank you again.
